newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK Telecom eyes securitisation.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - HK Telecom eyes securitisation.

text.p: Hongkong Telecom announced on Thursday that it had chosen Societe Generale to arrange a floating rate note issue backed by mortgages held by Hongkong Telecom for its staff.
Meanwhile, in the continuing Thailand Yankee saga, U.S. syndicate managers and investors expect good demand for the issue despite Moody's downgrade of Thailand's sovereign debt.

Moody's Investors Service on Wednesday cut Thailand to A3 from A2. Standard and Poor's Corp has kept Thailand at single-A on the grounds that the sad state of Thailand's financial sector will not adversely affect the country's creditworthiness.
As expected, S&P has rated Thailand's US$500 million Yankee single-A.
U.S. traders said the uncertain U.S. interest rate environment would have more impact on demand for the issue than Thailand's rating woes.
Price talk continues to center around 85-90 basis points over Treasuries for the 10-year tranche, which is expected to be more popular than a longer-dated issue.
Hongkong Telecom has joined the small group of mortgage holders in Hong Kong that have chosen to securitise mortgage loans in order to free up capital.
The company has mandated Societe Generale to arrange a HK$800 million floating rate note issue backed by mortgage loans held for Hongkong Telecom staff.
The issue will be fully guaranteed by AAA-rated MBIA Assurance S.A. As a result, the notes are expected to receive an AAAr rating from S&P and Aaa from Moody's.
The notes' average life is estimated at approximately five years.

In March, Sino Commercial Properties Funding launched through Morgan Stanley International a US$300 million Euro-Asian FRN backed by commercial mortgages in Hong Kong owned by property developer Sino Land.
The notes, which have an expected final of five years, paid a discount margin of 90 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate.

In related debt news, China will shortly allow selected state firms to issue four billion yuan (US$481.9 million) worth of convertible bonds as part of its efforts to push forward reform of the state sector, a Shanghai newspaper reported today.
China previously had allowed only a handful of listed firms to issue convertible bonds.
